DAY-BEFORE / 24-48H CHECKS (quick hits)
- Validate Dedicated pool health dashboard (console > Dedicated > Pool-5). Look for 90th pct latency spike > 20% vs baseline. If spike: page SRE and tag 'pool-5'.
- Confirm model pin assignments for weekend rollouts: model = rwx-v2-quant, pinned to image-2026-02-28. Cross-check with model-catalog ticket.
- Ensure canary capacity reserved: 3 instances w/ low-priority burst. If not reserved, open ticket to infra (email infra-runbooks).
- Verify last smoke-run results (smoke/last-run.json) — critical checks: health endpoints, prefix caching, stream stability. Mark any failing check with TODO.

MEETING AGENDA (for my 10–15 min run)
1) Quick status (30s each): Hosted API, Dedicated, Private — 3 bullet lines max.
2) Go/No-Go candidate items (3) — call out owner for decision.
3) High-risk regressions & mitigations (A/B, rollbacks, fallback).
4) Open action items from last week (owners + ETA).
5) Escalations and customer-impacting items.

GO/NO-GO CHECKLIST (my shorthand)
- Safety: latest canary passed golden prompt set? [yes/no] — if no -> NO-GO and block rollout. Owner: Priya.
- Latency: 95th <= SLO (hosted) and Dedicated 90th within committed window? [ok/warn/fail] Owner: Jordan.
- Throughput: capacity test at target qps for model variant (rwx-v2-quant) >= 90% predicted. Owner: Marco (perf eng).
- Telemetry: traces + logs flowing to observability (no gaps > 5 min). Owner: Observability on-call.
- Rollback plan: image rollback verified in staging (time-to-recover < 10m). Owner: me (Aisha) — pre-check: rehearse command set.

LIVE-RUN CUES (during shiproom)
- If latency alert fires: call out metric, ask SRE to confirm impact (hosted vs dedicated). If impact is hosted only -> consider global throttles, otherwise trigger capacity burst.
- If canary fails: pause rollout, gather failing prompts, escalate to Applied ML for quality triage. Capture failing prompt examples in the meeting notes.
- If control plane flaps: deploy cross-region fallback policy, set communication to CS + site-status.

SMOKE-TEST QUICK-LOOK (ordered)
1) /health (all regions) — expect 200 and healthy=true.
2) golden prompt generation (3 variants) — check for coherent output and stable token length.
3) streaming socket smoke (5 simulated clients) — no connection resets.
4) KV cache hit-rate sanity check (> 30% for typical workloads).
5) auth flow: token validation for dev key and prod key.

RISKS I CARE ABOUT (notes to self)
- Quantized model edge cases: hallucinations on long-context prompts unseen in evals. Watch for uptick in hallucination rate on live eval monitors.
- Autoscale cold starts: small percentage of cold starts can push P95 over threshold. Keep warmup policy on for first 2h post-deploy.
- Third-party infra patch windows (cloud provider) could impact Dedicated zones — pre-check weekly maintenance calendar.

OPEN ACTIONS (make sure to call out in meeting)
- A1: Priya — re-run golden prompt suite with latest model (due 2026-03-03). Status: running.
- A2: Jordan — validate Dedicated pool latency anomaly root cause, post short RCA (due 2026-03-05). Status: investigating.
- A3: Marco — confirm scaling headroom numbers for expected QPS spike; provide conservative headroom estimate (due 2026-03-04).
- A4: Aisha (me) — rehearse rollback commands in staging and record exact steps in private playbook (due 2026-03-02).
- A5: Eng-sre on-call — add trace tag for canary requests to make debugging faster (due 2026-03-03).

NOTES-TO-SELF / RUN-TIME SNIPPETS
- Keep the Launch Channel pinned and set ephemeral notifications: only @here for major go/no-go decisions.
- One-sentence status template for quick updates: "Area — short-state (ok/warn/fail) — top-1 mitigation if warn/fail". Use this when I call status.
- If we need to delay: propose a 1-hour cool-down + redo canary after fixes.

ESCALATION CONTACTS (quick)
- SRE on-call (pager): pager.sre@redwood.internal — send with subject: "shiproom: [area] [short tag]"
- Applied ML: priya.nair@redwood.com (for model-quality escalations)
- Infra runbook slack: #infra-runbooks (use slash /runbook deploy-rollback)

POST-MEETING FOLLOW-UP FORMAT (what I send to channel)
- TL;DR (1 line)
- Decisions (go/no-go + what changed)
- Owners + actions (one-line per action with ETA)
- Customer-facing items (any comms to CS + suggested text)

EXAMPLE QUICK COMMS (copyable)
- "TL;DR: Go for staged rollout (canary ok). Action: Priya to finish regression suite; Jordan to monitor Dedicated P95. Aisha to coordinate rollback rehearsal."
- "Customer note (for CS): We observed intermittent latency in Dedicated pool during preflight; mitigation is increased warmup and a temporary capacity bump. ETA for final fix: 48h."

MY PERSONAL CHECKLIST BEFORE HAND-OFF
- Confirm notes & action items added to central release tracker (JIRA-RELEASE-2026).
- Make sure ownership is explicit (no ambiguous "eng team" lines).
- Leave a 15-min buffer after the meeting for async follow-ups and handover to ops.

FRAGMENTS / THINGS I WANT TO INVESTIGATE (later)
- Can we automate the canary prompt selection so it's representative of top-100 queries? (pitch to applied-ml)
- Metric to add: per-model hallucination delta vs baseline (daily) — needs logging hook.
- Explore a one-click rollback UI in console for small teams (longer-term product ask).

END-OF-DAY LOG (fill after shiproom)
- Outcome: [GO / NO-GO] — notes: _____
- Actions I triggered: list with timestamps
- Follow-ups I delegated: list with owner + ETA

(Misc scratch lines)
- remember: breathe. keep the meeting short. if debate > 3min, move to async deep-dive.

Summary
-------
This document defines the cross-organizational go-live protocol used by Redwood Inference for enterprise tenant cutovers. It focuses on communications, stakeholder coordination, and an escalation ladder tailored for high-risk or high-visibility customers. Use this runbook as the canonical checklist for the 72 hours before, during, and 72 hours after a cutover where multiple teams (Customer Success, SRE, Solutions Engineering, Product, and Sales) must be coordinated.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: Dedicated and Private deployment go-lives and tenant migrations with SLA commitments (any customer with an enterprise contract or > $50k monthly spend).
- Out of scope: self-serve trial accounts, routine model-only updates without routing changes.

Goals and SLOs to Protect
-------------------------
- Availability SLA target to protect during cutover: 99.9% (monthly) for production routes.
- Immediate remediation thresholds (trigger escalation):
  - Error rate spike: sustained >5% errors for 5 minutes across tenant endpoints.
  - Latency spike: P95 latency >2000ms for 10 minutes.
  - Token cost anomaly: >200% of projected token spend in 30 minutes.
  - KV cache miss-rate >30% sustained for 15 minutes (for cache-sensitive workloads).

Pre-Cutover (T-72 to T-1 hours)
-------------------------------
1. Confirm stakeholders and channels
   - Primary CSM (Customer Success Manager): name + mobile number.
   - Tech lead (Customer): contact + escalation path.
   - Solution Engineer (SE): responsible for ingress, API contract verification.
   - Oncall SRE/Platform owner: PagerDuty schedule and runbook owner.
   - Slack channels: #cs-<customer>-go-live (private channel), #oncall-redwood, #se-ops.
2. Telemetry sanity checks — must pass before proceeding:
   - Synthetic journey (happy path) passes end-to-end: <customer> -> Redwood API -> response < 1s.
   - PromQL checks: error_rate/instance < 0.005 for 10m; p95_latency_query < 1500ms.
3. Canary plan and acceptance criteria
   - Canary traffic: route 1% of production for 30 minutes with zero critical errors.
   - Acceptance: no P0/P1 incidents during canary and no regression in model quality metrics (if applicable).
4. Whitelist and firewall confirmations
   - Verify ingress IP ranges, customer egress rules, and TLS client certs.

During Cutover (T0 to +4 hours) — Immediate Checklist
----------------------------------------------------
- Primary communications protocol:
  - All updates posted to #cs-<customer>-go-live every 10 minutes during the first hour, then every 30 minutes until stable.
  - The CSM posts customer-facing status updates; technical details posted to private channel only.
- Live monitoring dashboard (owner: Oncall SRE):
  - Tenant-specific dashboard showing throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, KV cache hits, token consumption.
- Escalation triggers (first responder must escalate within 5 minutes if triggered):
  1) P0: service unavailable for customer routes — immediate page to P1 oncall and notify Engineering Director.
  2) P1: sustained SLO breach (see thresholds above) — page SE and PM, start RCA and mitigation steps.
  3) P2: model quality regression detected — notify Applied ML and SE; consider traffic switch to verified model snapshot.

Escalation Ladder (contact order and responsibilities)
----------------------------------------------------
| Level | Trigger example | Primary contact | Secondary contact | Action required |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (CSM) | Customer questions, minor errors | CSM | SE | Acknowledge to customer within 15m, open internal thread |
| L2 (SRE) | Error rate >5% | Oncall SRE | SRE Lead | Execute diagnostics, apply mitigations (rate-limit, route switch) |
| L3 (SE/PM) | Persistent degradation >30m | Solutions Engineer | Product Manager | Coordinate config changes, model fallback, communicate to customer executives |
| L4 (Exec) | SLA breach or major incident | Head of Customer Success | Head of Engineering | Declare incident, engage legal/finance if SLA credits likely |

Note: The table above is intended as a quick reference. The full escalation paging list with phone numbers and PagerDuty IDs is stored in /confluence/people-ops/rosters and in the private channel pinned messages.

Common Mitigations (ordered by lowest customer impact first)
----------------------------------------------------------
- Increase routing to a higher-capacity pool (if Dedicated: burst pool)
- Apply tenant-level throttles to protect shared resources (quota reduce to 30% of projected steady-state)
- Enable model fallback: route to last-known-stable model snapshot
- Temporarily switch customer to hosted API endpoint (if allowed by contract)
- Quiesce long-running batch jobs from the customer side

Rollback and Safe-fail Strategies
--------------------------------
1. Safe rollback to previous routing config (SE executes):
   - Command: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal.redwood/v1/route/revert -d '{"tenant":"<tenant-id>","to_config":"<previous-config-id>"}' 
   - Confirm routing table via: kubectl get svc ingress-<tenant> -o yaml (requires ops role)
2. Tenant quiesce API (customer-facing graceful shutdown):
   - POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/tenants/<tenant>/quiesce?actor=ops
   - Expected behavior: existing requests drain, new requests return 429 with Retry-After header.
3. Emergency switchback to hosted region: update DNS TTL and apply traffic policy TTL=30s for faster re-routing.

Communication Templates
-----------------------
- Customer-facing 1-line (acknowledge): "We are investigating increased latency for your production routes and will provide an update within 15 minutes. No action required from your side unless we ask."
- Customer-facing status update (10m cadence): include short bullet list: observed metric, action taken, owner, ETA for next update.
- Internal P0 page message sample:
  - "P0: <customer> production routes returning 503s since 08:12 UTC. Oncall SRE investigating. Initial hypothesis: ingress proxy thread exhaustion. Paging SRE Lead and SE. Next update in 5 minutes"

Telemetry checks / Queries (examples)
----------------------------------
- PromQL (errors): sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[5m])) > 0.05
- Token consumption anomaly (example):
  - Query: increase(token_count_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[30m]) / expected_token_rate > 2.0
- Synthetic validation command (curl):
  - curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -d '{"input":"synthetic health check"}' | jq '.latency_ms'

Post-Cutover (T+4 to T+72 hours)
--------------------------------
- Stability window monitoring: SRE to keep watch for 72 hours; escalate on any SLO breach.
- Cost and quota reconciliation: Finance Ops and CSM to review token consumption, forecast delta, and apply quota protections if needed.
- Customer QBR prep: collect first-week metrics and any incident notes for the 30-day QBR.

Runbook Ownership and RACI
-------------------------
- CSM: customer comms and executive escalation.
- SE: onboarding technical lead, API contract signoff, whitelist verification.
- Oncall SRE: monitoring, mitigation, and platform config changes in emergencies.
- Product/Applied ML: model quality regressions and rollbacks.
- Finance Ops: post-cutover cost anomalies and quota adjustments.

Appendix A — Playbook Checklist (copyable)
-----------------------------------------

- [ ] Firewall/whitelist config validated by Network team

- [ ] Post-cutover QBR slot scheduled with customer (within 30 days)

Appendix B — Links and References
--------------------------------
- Tenant cutover checklist (internal): /confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-handback-and-first-90-days-ops-guide-2026
- Incident comms templates: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-communication-templates
- PagerDuty runbook: https://pagerduty.com/orgs/redwood-incidents (private)

Appendix C — Escalation Contact Quickview
----------------------------------------
- Oncall SRE: pagerduty (PD ID: PD12345), Slack: @oncall-sre, mobile: +1-555-0102
- SE on duty: Slack: @se-ops, mobile: +1-555-0148
- CSM (Primary): Priya Patel, Slack: @priya.cs, mobile: +1-555-0190

Revision History
----------------

- 2027-03-02: Reviewed and clarified rollback steps; added expense reconciliation task (Marisol Gomez).

Notes and governance
--------------------
Keep this page updated after every enterprise go-live. If the customer contract contains additional communication obligations (e.g., weekly executive summaries), add them to the post-cutover tasks and pin them in the customer channel.

Summary
-------
This playbook describes a repeatable process for converting observed runtime workload signatures into defensible Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and cost-sensitivity profiles for Redwood inference services. It ties together sampling, profiling, experiment design, and SLO derivation so teams can make consistent, evidence-based SLOs for new routes, model variants, and capacity plans.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all inference-facing HTTP/streaming routes and internal RPCs that contribute to model-serving latency or cost. Excludes: purely offline batch jobs (see eng-infra runbooks) and human-in-the-loop lab experiments.

Definitions
-----------
- Workload signature: a compact description of request shape and distribution (sequence length percentiles, batching patterns, KV cache hit ratio, request concurrency, special flags like streaming or tool-calls).
- Cost-sensitivity: the change in per-request GPU/time cost when a workload attribute shifts (e.g., +10 tokens => +X ms / +Y token-cost).
- SLO bucket: a named target (e.g., P95 latency 120ms for interactive, P99 500ms for high-throughput) tailored for a workload class.

Key Principles
--------------
- Evidence-first: SLOs must be justified by sampled production telemetry and controlled experiments.
- Workload-driven segmentation: avoid one-size-fits-all SLOs; segment by signature clusters that materially change cost/latency.
- Cost-aware guardrails: every SLO must include an associated cost-sensitivity statement used for tradeoff decisions (e.g., whether to enable larger batch sizes or fallback to cheaper model variants).
- Operational observability: each derived SLO must have dashboards, automated alerts, and an attached experiment plan for periodic revalidation.

Procedure: Derive SLOs from workload signatures (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------------------------------
1. Collect signatures (1–2 weeks):
   - Instrument route to emit compact signature blobs at sampling rate 1–5% (configurable per traffic volume). Required fields: route_id, timestamp, seq_len, input_tokens, output_tokens, kv_cache_hit, streaming_flag, client_tier, model_variant_hint.
   - Example signature JSON (emit to telemetry):

   {
     "route_id": "generate-chat",
     "timestamp": "2025-10-28T14:12:33Z",
     "seq_len": 1024,
     "input_tokens": 128,
     "output_tokens": 256,
     "kv_cache_hit": 0.62,
     "streaming_flag": false,
     "client_tier": "standard"
   }

2. Cluster signatures (offline job):
   - Run k-means / hierarchical clustering on normalized features: seq_len, total_tokens, kv_cache_hit, streaming_flag (binary), concurrency_hint. Aim for 3–6 clusters per route unless variance indicates more.
   - Save cluster centroids and representative percentiles (p50/p90/p99) for each numeric field.

3. Profile representative clusters (controlled experiments):
   - For each cluster, replay 10k representative requests against target model variants and runtime configurations (batch sizes, quantization profiles, kernel paths). Collect: p50/p90/p99 latencies, tail latency (p999), token throughput, GPU utilization, memory pressure, failure rate.
   - Record cost-per-request estimate (energy + GPU time + amortized infra) using the internal cost-modeler.

4. Construct candidate SLO buckets:
   - Use profiling results to propose SLOs that are achievable with a 95% confidence margin given current infra. Example logic: set P95 latency target to profiling p90 + 15% buffer; set error-rate target to observed mean + 3σ but not exceeding 1%.

5. Attach cost-sensitivity and fallback policy:
   - For each SLO, include a table showing how latency and cost change when you: increase batch_by, enable quantization Q4/Q5, or downgrade to smaller model variant.
   - Define automatic fallback thresholds (e.g., if queue length > 200 and P95 approaching target, route 20% to cheaper variant).

6. Review and publish with runbook:
   - Include owners (service, infra, SRE), approval from product for user-facing impact, and security sign-off when signatures include user data.

7. Deploy SLO and monitor:
   - Create dashboards that show per-cluster SLI trends, cost-per-1000-requests, and deviation from target. Configure alerts: SLO_red (p95 > target for 10m), SLO_yellow (p95 > 90% of target for 15m), cost_alert (cost growth > 20% week-over-week for the cluster).

Representative table: sample SLO derivation for a chat-gen route
----------------------------------------------------------------
| Cluster | Centroid seq_len (p90) | Profiling p95 | Proposed SLO (p95) | Cost/request | Fallback action |
|---------|------------------------:|-------------:|-------------------:|-------------:|-----------------|
| Short-turn | 64 | 80 ms | 95 ms | $0.0009 | no fallback, optimize batching |
| Normal | 256 | 160 ms | 190 ms | $0.0021 | enable burst batching or route 10% to smaller model |
| Long-turn | 1024 | 420 ms | 500 ms | $0.0065 | enable quantization Q4 + degrade non-critical tools |

(When converting to Confluence markup, render as a table with exact values and links to profiling runs.)

Cost-sensitivity matrix (example)
--------------------------------
- Changing batch_size from 1 -> 8 on `Normal` cluster: +20% p95, -30% cost/request.
- Enabling Q4 quantization on `Long-turn`: +12% p95, -45% cost/request, memory drop 18%.

Operational playbook snippets
---------------------------
- When an SLO_red fires (p95 > target for 10m):
  1. Pager to oncall (SRE) and service owner.
  2. Run the quick triage checklist: confirm signature cluster involved, verify ongoing experiment/rollout, check GPU node saturation and preemption events.
  3. If saturation: trigger temporary priority decay policy and increase fallthrough to cheaper variant per SLO fallback policy.
  4. Post-incident: schedule a 2-hour root-cause session and update SLO derivation if recurring.

Best practices and guidance
---------------------------
- Prefer cluster-specific SLIs rather than global route-level; combine for a user-facing composite only when necessary.
- Maintain an experiment repository: every profiling run must have a reproducible seed, input corpus, model hash, and runtime flags.
- Re-derive SLAs quarterly or when a model variant, kernel path, or major infra change is shipped.
- Use conservative buffers for user-facing production routes (15–25%) and tighter buffers for internal tooling (5–10%).

  --input s3://redwood-telemetry/signatures/generate-chat/2025-10/

description:
Summary: Introduces a new variance-aware autoscaler that factors request-rate variance and burstiness into scale decisions and burst token allocation. This is targeted at intermittent-surge workloads (spiky, short-lived bursts from many tenants) where standard utilization-based autoscaling either overreacts or under-allocates burst capacity. Motivation: We observed several support incidents where tenants with highly variable arrival patterns caused oscillation in node counts and unfair consumption of burst tokens, degrading tail latency for other tenants. This change aims to reduce oscillation, make burst distribution fairer across tenants, and provide observability to tune policies. Key components: 1) controller/autoscaler/variance_controller.go: new controller that computes per-tenant mean and variance over a sliding window, derives an "effective demand" metric combining 95th percentile rate and variance penalty, and exposes decisions to the scaling plane; 2) pkg/scheduler/fair_burst_allocator.go: integrates variance metric into burst token allocation algorithm, preferring tenants with consistently high short-term variance to receive temporary soft credits while enforcing tenant-level fairness caps; 3) pkg/telemetry/metrics_exporter.go: new Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboard templates for per-tenant request variance, effective_demand, burst_credit_usage, and burst_credit_hitrate; 4) cmd/controller-manager/main.go: wires the new controller behind a feature flag (--enable-variance-autoscaler); 5) helm/charts/autoscaler/templates/: adds config options for sliding window length, variance weight, and maximum soft burst per-tenant. Design notes: - Effective demand = alpha * p95_rate + beta * sqrt(variance), where alpha and beta are tunable. Default alpha=1.0, beta=0.5. - Hysteresis and cooldown: dynamic cooldown scales with variance to avoid thrash: cooldown = base_cooldown + gamma * normalized_variance. - Burst fairness uses a time-decayed ledger so transient spikes don't permanently drain credits. Tests and CI: unit tests added for variance estimator, allocator fairness invariants, and edge cases (zero-traffic, constant traffic, synthetic heavy-tail spikes). Integration test added in perf-canary suite simulating 1k tenants with exponentially distributed spike arrivals to validate stability and tail latency. CI: all checks passed after two iterations (lint, unit, integration perf-lite). Rollout plan: gated behind --enable-variance-autoscaler and feature gate variance_autoscaler_v1. Step 1: deploy to canary clusters with default beta=0.5 and monitor metrics for 48h. Step 2: if tail latency improves and no regressions, enable in staging clusters. Step 3: gradual rollout to Dedicated fleet with telemetry-backed rollback triggers (burst_credit_hitrate drop or node oscillation rate > threshold). Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged when feature flag disabled. Migration: none. Observability and dashboards: new Grafana panels added (per-tenant variance heatmap, effective_demand distribution, burst_credit_consumption by tenant percentile). Performance impact: controller runs O(N) over active tenants; optimized with shard workers and sampling for large clusters. Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - We intentionally use sqrt(variance) to keep units closer to rate while still reflecting variability. - To limit overhead, high-cardinality tenant metrics are aggregated into percentiles by default; full per-tenant metrics are optional via config. - There is a small potential for temporary unfairness during burst draining windows; the time-decayed ledger mitigates this. Links: Related Linear tasks ENG-3492 (variance estimator), ENG-3620 (fair allocator integration). Related PRs: none.

This caused duplicate tool invocations, incorrect schema inference, and brittle downstream tool routers in Redwood Dedicated/Private deployments.

This PR introduces a deterministic normalization step for the OpenAI invocation envelope, plus stream-resilient framing for tool/message fragments. The goal is to: 1) make the compatibility layer emit a single canonical selection signal for every invocation, 2) map OpenAI tool schemas into a stable internal schema with minimal changes for existing customers, and 3) make streaming fragments idempotent and re-assemblable at the service edge.

What changed (high level):
- New package: pkg/openai/normalize_invocation.go — normalizer that transforms incoming OpenAI-style responses into Redwood's canonical InvocationEnvelope. It collapses multiple tool signals into one selected_tool hint and preserves tool confidence/metadata in a stable metadata map.
- Tool schema mapper: pkg/tooling/tool_schema_mapper.go — conservative mapping rules for OpenAI 'parameters' -> Redwood typed schema, including type coercion rules and a small whitelist for nested objects.
- Streaming: server/streaming/frame_parser.go updated to add fragment IDs and checksum headers for tool/message fragments. Parser now supports out-of-order fragments and dedup by fragment id+checksum.
- API layer: server/api/openai_adapter.go updated to call the normalizer before routing to tool routing pipeline; updates to response shape sent back to clients to maintain OpenAI wire-compatibility while ensuring a single 'selected_tool' semantic in the internal router.
- Docs: docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md with migration notes and examples.

Compatibility notes:
- Outbound API responses remain OpenAI-compatible: we do not change the visible OpenAI fields returned to customers. Internally, however, the runtime will prefer the normalized 'selected_tool' hint to decide which tool to invoke. In the rare case of conflicting tool signals, the normalizer uses (in order): explicit_invocation field, highest-confidence tool_choice, then deterministic fallback to first available tool that matches schema.
- Customers who implemented custom tool routers based on raw tool_choice fragments should migrate to using the new normalized hint or consult the docs which show a 1-line change to switch to the normalized envelope.

- Unit tests for mapping rules and type coercions included.
- Integration tests: simulated streaming sessions with fragmented tool metadata; verified idempotent assembler under network reorders.

During a staggered canary rollout for rw-instruct-7b-v3 in us-east-1, NimbleApps reported ~12% of their requests being served by an older model variant despite an explicit tenant-level model pin. The behavior lasted for ~45 minutes and coincided with an autoscaler prewarm burst triggered by a traffic spike.

Impact:
- Customer reported mixed outputs and downstream feature regressions for active users (measured anomalous quality score increase and user complaints).
- Approximately 11k requests affected for the customer across the incident window.

Environment:
- Production, us-east-1, Dedicated pool for NimbleApps (reserved capacity pool id: ded-342)

2025-11-02 Priya Singh (Support): Customer opened chat reporting that a portion of requests are returning legacy responses after we started the canary. They provided request IDs and timestamps. Asked to triage asap.
2025-11-02 Liam Chen (SRE): Acknowledged; collecting edge logs and routing snapshots. Initial hypothesis: pin commit race between orchestrator commit and edge cookie rotation during prewarm handoff.
2025-11-03 SRE-team (Liam Chen): Found routing mesh epochs where cohort snapshot contained mixed variant entries for tenant nimbleapps-17. Edge logs show affinity cookie TTL renewal at the same second as prewarm probe success; some flows lost pin before orchestrator snapshot completed.
2025-11-04 Support (Priya Singh) -> Customer: Confirmed we are rolling a targeted hotfix that changes prewarm handshake ordering to commit pins before edge cookie rotation. Asked customer for traffic window to cutover safely.
2025-11-05 NimbleApps (Customer): Verified behaviour has ceased after cutover; provided sampling confirming no legacy outputs in a 1h window post-fix. Thanked on call for quick turnaround.

investigation_notes:
What we observed:
- Autoscaler prewarm created N new prewarm nodes at t0+12s in response to surge.
- Prewarm handshake had a non-atomic ordering: node marked healthy -> edge cookie rotation -> orchestrator snapshot commit.
- In ~9% of sampled requests, edge rotated tenant affinity cookie just before orchestrator committed the new pin mapping, causing requests to land on edge shards that still resolved the tenant to the legacy variant.
- Orchestrator snapshots showed an overlapping epoch where two different routing tables were readable by different edge shards for ~18s.
- No GPU OOMs or serving runtime crashes found. Latency remained within SLO except for slight tail increase during the handoff window.

Hypotheses considered and eliminated:
- Tokenization mismatch in the model: rejected after verifying request payloads and embeddings.
- Customer-side pinned version misconfiguration: rejected; tenant manifest showed explicit pin to rw-instruct-7b-v3 prior to rollout.

Contributing factors:
- Prewarm handshake ordering (health -> rotate cookie -> commit) is non-atomic across control-plane and edge.
- Edge cookie rotation TTL is short and coincided with the commit window during a burst.
- Canary scheduling used staggered slice times (0s, +10s, +20s) which increased overlap surface for commit windows across shards.

resolution_notes:
Immediate mitigations applied:
1) Rolled a hotfix to orchestrator to change prewarm handshake ordering: commit pin mapping before issuing edge cookie rotation. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/3184. Deployed to us-east-1 dedicated pools at 2025-11-04T04:00Z.
2) Increased health-probe smoothing for prewarm nodes to reduce transient epoch changes during bursts.
3) Added a guard in edge-proxy to prefer orchestrator pin mapping when epoch differences detected within a 30s window.

Rollout notes:
- Hotfix applied via canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%) over a 3-hour window for dedicated pools; monitored cohort pins and customer telemetry.
- Post-deployment checks (logs + sampling from NimbleApps) showed 0% legacy-routed requests in the 1h stable window.

Follow-ups and action items:

- Create a capacity-surge playbook to avoid staggered slice overlap during autoscaler prewarm (owner: Product, target: 2025-11-20).
- Postmortem scheduled and linked: https://confluence.redwood.ai/postmortems/SUP-209876-postmortem

Customer communication:
- Notified NimbleApps via support and scheduled an incident review call. Customer confirmed remediation and accepted workaround as final resolution.

description:
Context and motivation: Private-installer releases consume artifacts produced by multiple build pipelines (core runtime, helm charts, terraform modules, third-party vendor artifacts). This PR extends the release index generation to aggregate origin provenance across repos/pipelines so operators can inspect where each artifact came from and verify chain-of-custody at install time.

What this PR does: - Adds an `origins` aggregate block to the release index JSON that lists source repository, pipeline job id, build commit, and optional SBOM/cosign references per artifact. - Modifies the private-installer indexer job to query multiple artifact registries and cross-reference artifact digests to upstream build metadata (via the new origin-mapper service). - Adds origin-mapper microservice (lightweight Go lambda) that merges build metadata across internal buildkite/jenkins/job-run APIs and returns a normalized origin statement for an artifact digest. - Updates CI/CD pipelines: new step in release pipeline to call origin-mapper and attach signed origin blobs to TUF/manifest staging area. - Enhances verification: indexer validates cosign signatures on origin blobs (if present) and records signature verification result in the index. - Adds operator docs and an index API example in private-installer docs for auditors to query artifact origins during upgrades/rollbacks.

Commits (high-level): - feat(indexer): add origin mapping hooks and schema v2 metadata - feat(origin-mapper): initial service with buildkite and jenkins adapters - ci(release): add origin-stage and sign-origin steps, upload to staging TUF area - docs(installer): add operator guide and example queries - test(integration): multi-repo origin aggregation smoke test - fix(ci): tolerate missing SBOM references for third-party mirrored artifacts

Files/areas changed (high-level): - private-installer/cmd/indexer: indexer changed to call origin-mapper and persist origins into index JSON - private-installer/internal/index/schema_v2.go: new schema and JSON marshaling changes - tools/origin-mapper/: new Go service and adapters for buildkite/jenkins - infra/ci/pipelines/release.yml: added origin-stage, sign-origin and upload steps - docs/private-installer/origins.md: operator documentation and API examples - charts/private-installer/values.yaml: small annotation for chart provenance - scripts/dev/replay-origins.sh: local dev helper to simulate upstream metadata

This PR implements a dynamic per-channel requant stage combined with a KV-cache-aware scheduling hint and a jitter-resilient continuous-batching policy to smooth throughput while keeping low tail latency. Scope: 1) A lightweight per-channel scale estimator that runs on the microkernel hot path and updates requant multipliers at configurable amortization windows. 2) A cheap, lock-free KV cache sizing hint that the scheduler uses to avoid abrupt prefix evictions during batch coalescing. 3) A jitter-resilient continuous-batcher that introduces minimal, adaptive hold windows to align requests from high-variance sources without increasing median latency. 4) Microkernel changes to expose a fused transform that applies requant multipliers inline with dequant/attn input packing to eliminate an extra copy. The placement layer still enforces hard SLOs; the hint avoids placing requests that would cause a working-set jump on the same GPU within a short window. - Batcher employs an adaptive jitter budget: it only delays the head of a queue by up to X ms if the expected throughput improvement outweighs the added latency; X decays if p99 latency rises. This draft defines the design and staged rollout plan for an "attestation-aware" secrets gateway for private (VPC / on-prem) deployments. The gateway centralizes secret distribution and enforces hardware-backed key operations (HSM/KMS) combined with node attestation. The focus is operational hardening: key management patterns, secrets lifecycle, terraform module recommendations, upgrade and rollback procedures, and audit/logging requirements for compliance.

Goals:
- Provide a single control plane for secrets that can interoperate with customer-managed HSMs (on-prem or cloud) and our KMS adapter.
- Enforce attestation-based release of DEKs to runtime nodes (VMs / containers) to ensure only verified hosts can unwrap keys.
- Minimize blast radius when migrating keys or upgrading modules; provide clear terraform migration steps and rollbacks.
- Produce tamper-evident audit trails and integrate with existing observability pipelines.

Non-goals:
- Implementing full PKI for customer environments (we rely on existing attestation providers: TPM, Nitro Enclaves, or GCP/AWS attestation services).
- Replacing customer HSM vendors; focus on interop and fallback.

High-level architecture (textual):
- Secrets Gateway (SG): stateless control plane deployed in customer VPC; authenticates operator and clusters, stores metadata only.
- KEK Manager: interacts with customer KMS/HSM via configured connectors (cloud KMS, network HSM, HSM appliance over PKCS#11). Holds only KEK references, not plaintext DEKs.
- DEK Store (encrypted): encrypted blob store (object store or vault) in customer environment; encrypted under KEK.
- Attestation Service: verifies node identity and health (TPM quote, cloud attestation token) and issues a short-lived attestation credential used to request DEK unwrapping.
- Secrets Agent (on node): requests DEKs from SG after presenting attestation token and mTLS identity; caches DEKs in memory with TTL + automatic wipe on signals.

Key flows:
1) Provisioning: Operator registers KEK connector in SG with PKCS#11 URI, connector credentials, key ID. Terraform-managed resource: redwood_secrets_kek_connector.
2) Secret write: Operator uploads secret to SG API; SG generates DEK (random), encrypts secret with DEK, calls KEK Manager to wrap DEK -> stores wrapped DEK + ciphertext in DEK store.
3) Node fetch: Node performs attestation -> obtains attestation token -> mTLS to SG -> SG validates attestation / policy -> asks KEK Manager to unwrap DEK (transient) -> returns plaintext DEK to SG just long enough to encrypt transport to node (or uses ECDH established session) -> node receives and decrypts secret locally.
4) Rotation: Operator triggers key rotation; new DEK generation and rewrap. Support rolling rewrap without downtime via dual-KEK acceptance window.

Operational hardening patterns:
- Always prefer HSM for KEK operations; configure offline HSM policies for high-sensitivity KEKs.
- Use split knowledge / dual-operator approval for KEK rotations on production class secrets.
- Enforce short attestation token lifetimes (<= 30s) and single-use tokens where backend supports it.
- Secrets Agent must zero memory on SIGTERM and provide explicit API to purge memory on SIGKILL tolerant platforms.
- Use envelope encryption: SG never persists plaintext DEKs to disk. Logs must redact all DEK plaintext.

Terraform module notes (recommendations):
- Module name: redwood/secrets-gateway/aws (or /gcp /onprem depending on provider). Keep provider-specific pieces behind small wrapper modules.
- Versioning: Semver for modules. Breaking changes only on major bump.

  variable \"deks_bucket\" { type = string }

- Lock provider versions and add explicit lifecycle rules to prevent accidental destroy: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on critical resources when env == "prod".

Upgrade and migration plan (high level):
- Preconditions: backups of wrapped-DEK blobs, KEK connector configuration exported, snapshot of SG configuration, full test suite passing in staging.
- Stage 1 (canary): Deploy new module to staging namespace; run end-to-end test where node attestation -> fetch -> decrypt cycle is exercised with staged HSM connector. Verify audit entries and metrics.
- Stage 2 (pilot): Deploy to one customer tenant (non-critical) or to one AZ within customer VPC. Use traffic shaping to limit live traffic and increase observability.
- Stage 3 (gradual rollout): For each customer region, perform a rolling gateway update with the following steps per region:
  1) terraform plan and review.
  2) terraform apply in canary subnet (1 instance). Verify attestation flow.
  3) Run rewrap test: generate test secret, rotate DEK, verify both old and new DEKs valid within acceptance window.
  4) Increase SG replicas and switch traffic.
  5) Remove old connectors after confirmation window.
- Rollback plan: keep previous module version in a branch that can be applied quickly. If unwrapping starts failing, immediately reverse to previous version and run a reconciliation script that rewraps any DEKs that were rekeyed under new KEK back to previous KEK, using backed-up plaintext OR via HSM facilitate multi-wrap (if available).

Terraform-specific migration steps (detailed):
- Step 0: Export current state: aws s3 cp s3://<deks-bucket>/metadata/backup-YYYYMMDD.json ./backup.json
- Step 1: Map existing KEKs to new terraform resource ids: create a mapping file (keystone-map.csv) with columns: existing_key_id, provider, suggested_tf_id.
- Step 2: Use terraform import for each KEK connector: terraform import module.sg.redwood_kek_connector["<tf_id>"] <existing_key_id>

Question:
Why did Northpeak Search see their Dedicated Burst Usage billed higher than expected, and how do we prevent retry attempts from double-counting burst GPU-seconds now?

Northpeak Search saw Dedicated Burst Usage come in higher than expected because the burst metering path was double-counting retries: when the client (and sometimes the gateway) retried on 429/overload or transient failures, the metering emitter produced a burst increment per attempt, and in some retry paths the request_id was regenerated per attempt while idempotency_key was missing/empty. Since downstream de-dupe was keyed mainly on (tenant_id, request_id), those attempts did not collapse, inflating daily burst GPU-seconds (notably 2025-06-15 to 2025-06-18).

To prevent this now, burst usage is made idempotent across retries by carrying a stable request-scoped idempotency key end-to-end: the gateway accepts X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key, and if absent generates a ULID once per incoming request and reuses it across internal retry attempts; the metering event includes idempotency_key, and the central burst_usage_aggregator dedupes on (tenant_id, region, hw_class, pool_id, idempotency_key) with a bounded TTL (storing only a hash of the key). We also added export-time reconciliation/guardrails (metrics for dropped duplicates and a batch check that alerts/blocks export if duplicate keys exceed a small threshold) and backfilled the affected dates with a billing adjustment/credit.

# Purpose
This page defines the **mandatory security controls** and **approval gates** for enabling **customer-managed audit log export** from Redwood Inference to customer-controlled cloud storage (e.g., S3/GCS/Azure Blob) across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

This is a control surface that touches: customer data boundaries, identity and access, encryption, and retention. **Do not enable export** without satisfying the requirements below.

# Scope
In scope:
- Export of **platform audit logs** (auth events, RBAC changes, API key lifecycle, console/admin actions, private control-plane actions).
- Delivery to a **customer-owned destination**.

Out of scope:
- Model inference payload logging (prompt/completion content). That remains disabled by default and requires a separate data logging exception.

# Definitions
- **Audit log**: event records emitted by Redwood control plane and selected data-plane components.
- **Customer-managed export**: Redwood pushes logs to an endpoint owned/controlled by the customer; the customer sets retention and access.
- **Export Connector**: Redwood-managed service that ships logs (see architecture page for details).

# Control requirements (must pass)
## 1) Data classification
- Audit logs are classified as **Customer-Sensitive Metadata**.
- Audit logs may include: user identifiers, IPs, org IDs, resource IDs, timestamps, and administrative actions.
- Audit logs must **not** include request bodies or model outputs.

## 2) Encryption
- In transit: TLS 1.2+ is required for any HTTPS endpoints.
- At rest: the customer destination must be configured with server-side encryption.
  - S3: SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS (customer preference).
  - GCS: Google-managed keys or CMEK.
  - Azure: Microsoft-managed keys or CMK.
- Redwood-side staging (if used by the connector) must be encrypted at rest using Redwood-managed KMS.

## 3) Least privilege access
- Hosted and Dedicated exports must use **assume-role / workload identity** patterns; no long-lived customer keys stored in Redwood.
- The role/policy must only permit:
  - write/put to a specific bucket/container prefix
  - list only if required by the connector health checks
- Policies must be reviewed by Security for correctness.

## 4) Network & destination allowlisting
- The destination must be customer-owned and reside in an allowed provider account/subscription/project per the contract.
- For Private deployments, outbound egress must be constrained by the customer (preferred) or by Redwood (if Redwood-managed networking is in scope).
- Public endpoints are allowed only if authenticated and protected with least-privilege credentials; **PrivateLink / private endpoints are preferred** when available.

## 5) Retention and deletion
- Default recommended destination retention: **90 days** (unless the customer requires more).
- If the customer requests retention < 30 days, note it in the request but it is allowed.
- If the customer requests retention > 1 year, Customer Success must confirm contract language supports it and that the customer understands storage cost/ownership.

## 6) Logging about logging (auditability of export)
- The platform must emit events for:
  - export enabled/disabled
  - destination changes (bucket/container/prefix)
  - auth/role changes used by the connector
  - delivery failures and retries
- These events must be visible in Redwood internal dashboards and retrievable for incident response.

# Approval gates (required)
## Gate A: Customer request validation (Customer Success + Support)
Required before Security review:
- customer company + deployment mode (Hosted / Dedicated / Private)
- target cloud + region
- desired log categories (standard only unless exception)
- retention intent
- contact for incident notifications

## Gate B: Security review (required for all modes)
Security must approve before any production enablement:
- destination configuration meets encryption and least privilege requirements
- no inference payload logging is included
- any cross-region delivery is evaluated (see Cross-region constraints)

Approval artifact:
- Jira internal-support ticket must include a Security comment: **“Approved for enablement”** with reviewer name + date.

## Gate C: Privacy/Legal check (conditional)
Required if any of the following are true:
- customer requests cross-region export that changes data residency guarantees
- customer requests inclusion of user email addresses or other PII fields beyond standard audit schema
- customer contract includes bespoke audit log clauses

# Cross-region constraints
- Default rule: **export must stay within the customer’s chosen region** that matches the deployment region.
- Cross-region export is allowed only when:
  1) Legal confirms it does not violate contractual residency terms
  2) Security confirms threat model is acceptable
  3) Customer acknowledges increased failure modes and latency

# Security exception process
If the customer cannot satisfy the above controls (e.g., insists on long-lived keys), file a Security exception under `security-and-compliance/risk-and-exceptions` and link it in the enablement ticket.

# Required evidence (attach/link in the Jira ticket)
- Destination policy snippet (IAM policy / role trust policy / workload identity binding)
- Confirmation of encryption at rest on destination
- Proof of ownership (account/subscription/project identifiers)
- For Private: network diagram or egress policy statement

- Dedicated customer setup runbook (Eng Infra)
